text_blocks.snippet: Heart disease, the leading cause of death for women, has several risk factors, some of which are unique to or more prevalent in women. These include traditional risk factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes, but also factors related to pregnancy, menopause, and certain autoimmune diseases. Lifestyle factors like smoking, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diet also significantly contribute to heart disease risk in women.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes, but also factors related to pregnancy, menopause, and certain autoimmune diseases

list.snippet: High Blood Pressure: Can damage and narrow arteries, increasing the risk of heart disease.
High Cholesterol: Leads to atherosclerosis, where plaque builds up in arteries.
Diabetes: Increases the risk of heart disease and can also cause nerve damage, potentially leading to silent heart attacks.
Smoking: Damages blood vessels and increases the risk of blood clots. Smoking is a greater risk factor for women than men.
Physical Inactivity: Worsens other risk factors like high blood pressure, cholesterol, and obesity.
Unhealthy Diet: High in saturated and trans fats, cholesterol, and sodium can contribute to heart disease and related conditions.
Obesity: Excess weight, particularly abdominal fat, increases the risk of heart disease.
Family History: Having a family history of heart disease, especially at a young age, increases your risk.
Pregnancy Complications: Conditions like preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, and preterm delivery can increase the risk of future cardiovascular problems.
Menopause: Lower estrogen levels after menopause can increase the risk of heart disease.
Autoimmune Diseases: Conditions like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis can increase inflammation and heart disease risk.
Depression and Stress: Mental health issues can negatively impact heart health and make it harder to manage other risk factors.
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): This condition is associated with an increased risk of heart disease.
Breast Cancer Treatment: Certain treatments, like radiation, can impact heart health.
